name: Lagwane (Kotoko de Logone-Birni)
place: Madiaco canton, Logone-Birni sultanate (Logone-et-Chari, Far North)
overview: The Lagwane, Kotoko of the sultanate of Logone-Birni, live from fishing and farming along the Logone, in symbiosis with the Massa, Mousgoum, Arabs and Kanuri. Heirs of the Sao, who came from Yemen via Sudan, Kanem-Bornu and Baguirmi, they honour the water goddess before the great fishing expeditions and dance the kounkouli when the sultan goes out.

sections.title: Identity and neighbours
items: Large group in the sultanate of Logone-Birni, integrated with all the peoples of the canton (Massa, Mousgoum, Arabs, Kanuri), whose languages it speaks.
Lagwan is also spoken in Chad and Nigeria.
Mixed marriages are the norm; the cultural mixing along the Logone makes the groups hard to tell apart.

sections.title: Territory and migrations
items: The site was that of the Sao ancestors.
Having set out from Yemen, the Lagwane passed through Sudan, Kanem-Bornou and Baguirmi, as far as Lake Chad.

sections.title: Social organisation and power
items: A sultan and several canton chiefs govern; decisions rise from the base to the top, where the sultan decides by consensus with the approval of his notables.
Bodies of the chiefdom, formerly permanent: warriors who restore peace, guardians of the princes who dress and enthrone the chief, nobles who decide and guardians of tradition who pass on messages.
All layers of society are represented at the chiefdom, so that no one feels excluded.
Unmarried people do not mix in public; the wife does not look at her husband and speaks to him crouching, with her back turned.

sections.title: Kinship, marriage and life passages
items: Patrilineal kinship; the woman joins her husband.
The boy becomes a man when he farms his own field; he marries at around 20-25. Formerly, girls were married very young.
Steps: observation of the girl's conduct, request to the parents, talks, engagement.
The kola nut publicly attests to the union, the bride price honours the young woman's parents, and clothes are offered; these expenses have increased greatly.

sections.title: Beliefs, sacred places and taboos
items: Before a big fishing expedition, the person in charge of the rite asked the water goddess for her favours.

Sacred places in the Lagwan language: vné ada, the “house of customs”, and vné miriwa at the palace; bana iba, at the palace; bana unemazolla, on the road to Kousseri; vné mahi; una dum, where sacrifices are made when fish is scarce. The monitor lizard and the snake are honoured there.
Birth is a great celebration; at death, “God gave, God has taken back”.
Adultery was punished by public beating and a fine; murder falls under State justice.
Each domain (fishing, enthronement…) has its ritual specialist.

sections.title: Economy, land and crafts
items: Men: fishing, farming. Women: pottery, market gardening, farming.
The land belongs to the men; it is accessed through the village chief or the sultan.
Crafts: weaving, sculpture, pottery for cooking.

sections.title: Clothing, health, beauty
items: Men: boubou, cloth belt; women: long flared dress and large veil (faille).
Traditional medicine remains in use for its effectiveness.
Beauty lies in conduct; seduction through elegance, dance, work, cleanliness and bearing.

sections.title: Music, dances and festivals
items: Music: royal kamkouli, liko, flute.
The kounkouli greets the sultan's coming out; the liko, a satirical song, is used to mock someone.
Festivals: AC Sao festival, Mouloud, Tabaski.

sections.title: History and cultural kinship
items: The cultural mixing along the Logone is such that Kotoko, Massa, Mousgoum and Kanuri are hard to tell apart.

sections.title: The names
items: Names depend on the circumstances of the birth, without a rite; they do not change.
Popular nicknames often make people forget the real names.
The founding ancestors are the Sao.

lessons.title: Who are the Lagwane (Kotoko de Logone-Birni)? Identity, language and territory
objectives: Name the Lagwane (Kotoko de Logone-Birni) community and explain its name
Locating your territory and its neighbours
Telling one's origin according to tradition
lessons.competence: Introduce the Lagwane (Kotoko de Logone-Birni) community (name, language, territory, neighbours, origin) and place it within the cultural diversity of Cameroon.
lessons.situation: A pen pal from another region asks you to introduce the Lagwane (Kotoko de Logone-Birni) community to them: who are they, where do they live, where do they come from?
lessons.materiel: Map of Cameroon, cultural profile of the community (“Cultures” section of Likalo).

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Present the Lagwane (Kotoko de Logone-Birni) community (name, language, territory, neighbours, origin) and place it within Cameroon's cultural diversity.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A pen friend from another region asks you to introduce the Lagwane (Kotoko de Logone-Birni) community to them: who are they, where do they live, where do they come from?” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What do the Lagwane (Kotoko de Logone-Birni) call themselves and what does this name mean? — What language do they speak, and where else is it spoken? — Which peoples do they live with? — Where did they come from, according to tradition?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present the following points, or have the students discover them: • Numerous group in the sultanate of Logone-Birni, integrated with all the peoples of the canton (Massa, Mousgoum, Arabs, Kanuri), whose languages it speaks. • Lagwan is also spoken in Chad and Nigeria. • Mixed marriages are the norm; the cultural mixing along the Logone makes the groups hard to tell apart. • The site was that of the Sao ancestors. • Setting out from Yemen, the Lagwane passed through Sudan, Kanem-Bornu and Baguirmi, as far as Lake Chad.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: The Lagwane, Kotoko of the sultanate of Logone-Birni, live from fishing and farming along the Logone, in symbiosis with the Massa, Mousgoum, Arabs and Kanuri. Heirs of the Sao, who came from Yemen via Sudan, Kanem-Bornu and Baguirmi, they honour the water goddess before the great fishing expeditions and dance the kounkouli when the sultan goes out.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: On a map of Cameroon, locate the Lagwane (Kotoko de Logone-Birni) community and its neighbours, then write 5 sentences to introduce it to your pen pal.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-II — Cultural practices: ways of life
lessons.title: Traditional food and drink of the Lagwane (Kotoko de Logone-Birni)
objectives: Linking food to the living environment
lessons.competence: Identify the traditional dishes and drinks of the Lagwane (Kotoko de Logone-Birni), describe how they are prepared and bring out their cultural significance.
lessons.situation: Your class is preparing a food fair. Your group must present a traditional dish of the Lagwane (Kotoko de Logone-Birni).
lessons.materiel: Cultural profile, pictures or local ingredients, display materials.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Identify the traditional foods and drinks of the Lagwane (Kotoko de Logone-Birni), describe their preparation and bring out their cultural significance.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “Your class is preparing a food fair. Your group has to present a traditional dish of the Lagwane (Kotoko de Logone-Birni).” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the main dishes and drinks? — What products are they made from? Where do these products come from? — Who prepares them, and on what occasions? — What do they say about the community's living environment?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • Traditional dishes: okra, lalo, sorrel, red millet and sorghum. • Drinks: tea, porridge. • Men: fishing, farming. Women: pottery, market gardening, farming.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: The Lagwane (Kotoko de Logone-Birni) eat mainly okra, lalo, sorrel, red millet and sorghum. Traditional drinks: tea, porridge. These foods are linked to the group's activities and to the products of its environment.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Choose a dish of the Lagwane (Kotoko de Logone-Birni): write its sheet (name in the language, ingredients, steps, occasion when it is served).

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Describe a Lagwane (Kotoko de Logone-Birni) dance (participants, time, instruments, gestures, meaning), then perform it with your group.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-IV — Cultural practices in communities (Level I)
lessons.title: Traditional economy and access to land among the Lagwane (Kotoko de Logone-Birni)
lessons.competence: Describe the economic activities of the Lagwane (Kotoko de Logone-Birni), the division of tasks between men and women and the rules of access to land.
lessons.situation: A development project wants to help the Lagwane (Kotoko de Logone-Birni). First it must understand how they work and who owns the land.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Describe the economic activities of the Lagwane (Kotoko de Logone-Birni), the division of tasks between men and women and the rules of access to land.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A development project wants to help the Lagwane (Kotoko de Logone-Birni). First it must understand how they work and who owns the land.” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the activities of men? of women? — Who owns the land and how is it accessed? — Which products are sold or exchanged? — Have these activities changed?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present the following points, or have the students discover them: • Men: fishing, farming. Women: pottery, market gardening, farming. • Land belongs to men; access is through the village chief or the sultan. • Crafts: weaving, carving, pottery for cooking.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Men: fishing, farming. Women: pottery, market gardening, farming. Land belongs to men; it is accessed through the village chief or the sultan.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Draw a two-column table (men / women) of the Lagwane (Kotoko de Logone-Birni)'s activities, then explain how land is accessed.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-V — Cultural practices in communities (Level II)
lessons.title: Beliefs, sacred places and taboos among the Lagwane (Kotoko de Logone-Birni)
objectives: Explain beliefs about life and death
lessons.competence: Explain the beliefs, sacred places and taboos of the Lagwane (Kotoko de Logone-Birni), and their role in regulating social life.
lessons.situation: A visitor arrives among the Lagwane (Kotoko de Logone-Birni). Which places and which rules must he absolutely respect?

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Explain the beliefs, sacred places and taboos of the Lagwane (Kotoko de Logone-Birni), and their role in regulating social life.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A visitor arrives among the Lagwane (Kotoko de Logone-Birni). Which places and which rules must they absolutely respect?” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the beliefs about birth and death? — Which places are sacred, and why? — What are the main taboos, and for whom? — How were serious offences atoned for?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following elements: • Before a big fishing expedition, the person in charge of the rite asked for the favours of the water goddess. • Sacred places in the Lagwan language: vné ada, the “hut of customs”, and vné miriwa at the palace; bana iba, at the palace; bana unemazolla, on the road to Kousseri; vné mahi; una dum, where sacrifices are made when fish is lacking. The monitor lizard and the snake are honoured there. • Birth is a great celebration; at death, “God gave, God has taken back”. • Adultery was punished by public caning and a fine; murder is a matter for State justice. • Each domain (fishing, enthronement…) has its ritual specialist.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Before a big fishing expedition, the person in charge of the rite asked the water goddess for her favours. Sacred places in the Lagwan language: vné ada, the “house of customs”, and vné miriwa at the palace; bana iba, at the palace; bana unemazolla, on the road to Kousseri; vné mahi; una dum, where sacrifices are made when fish are scarce. The monitor lizard and the snake are honoured there.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Write a short guide to good conduct for a visitor among the Lagwane (Kotoko de Logone-Birni) (3 places or rules to respect, with their reason).

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-V — Cultural practices in communities (Level II)
lessons.title: Greeting, introducing yourself and counting in Lagwan
lessons.anelcac: Traditional media and transmission: everyday language
objectives: Greeting according to the time of day

vocabulary.frenchText: morning greetings (as a sign of deference/respect)

lessons.competence: Use the greeting and introduction formulas of the Lagwane (Kotoko de Logone-Birni) and count from 1 to 10, respecting customs.
lessons.situation: You are visiting a Lagwane (Kotoko de Logone-Birni) family. Greet them, introduce yourself and take part in the sharing of kola nuts by counting.
lessons.materiel: Cultural profile (“Common expressions” and “Counting” sections), kola nuts or small objects.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Use the Lagwane (Kotoko de Logone-Birni) greeting and introduction formulas and count from 1 to 10, respecting customary usage.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “You are visiting a Lagwane (Kotoko de Logone-Birni) family. Greet them, introduce yourself and take part in the sharing of the cola nuts by counting.” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — How do you greet people depending on the time of day? — How do you introduce yourself (name, origin, place of residence)? — How do you count from 1 to 10? Is the system decimal, vigesimal…? — Why is language a tool of transmission?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present the following points, or have the students discover them: • The community's language is Lagwan. • Greeting formulae: ngul = Hello (neutral greeting, at any time of day); Baram sana = morning greeting (one person); Baran sana kun = morning greeting (several people). • Counting from 1 to 5: sehedia, sehested, ngaker, Gadé, Chechi. • The founding ancestors are the Sao. • The cultural mixing along the Logone is such that Kotoko, Massa, Mousgoum and Kanuri are hard to tell apart.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Greeting and counting in Lagwan are the first steps towards communicating with the Lagwane (Kotoko de Logone-Birni). The polite expressions convey the respect owed to people according to the time of day and their rank.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Role play in pairs: greet each other, introduce yourselves, ask where the other person comes from and count objects from 1 to 10.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

student.intro: Learn to greet, introduce yourself and count in Lagwan.

activities.title: I greet
activities.instruction: Learn the greeting formulas for morning, midday and evening.

activities.title: I introduce myself
activities.instruction: Say your name, where you are from and where you live.

activities.title: I count
activities.instruction: Count objects from 1 to 10.

activities.title: I pass on
activities.instruction: Teach a formula to a classmate or a family member.

student.memo: Greeting and counting in Lagwan are the first steps towards communicating with the Lagwane (Kotoko de Logone-Birni). The polite expressions convey the respect owed to people according to the time of day and their rank.
